Long, long ago, in the little town of Nazareth, there lived a kind young woman named Mary. She was engaged to a carpenter named Joseph — a skillful man with golden hands and a kind heart. They lived simply, happily, and full of love.

One day, wonderful news filled Mary's heart — the most important news of her whole life: she was going to have a very special son, one that the whole world was waiting for. Mary was surprised, and so happy, and she gently tucked this secret away safe in her heart.

In those days, an order went out: every family had to return to their hometown to be counted, so everyone could be written down by name. Joseph's hometown was Bethlehem. Well then, if they had to go, they had to go!

It was a long way to go—one hundred fifty kilometers! Mary rode on a little donkey, and Joseph walked beside her. By day the sun warmed them, and in the evening they rested by the roadside. And so, step by step, they made their way to Bethlehem.

But it seemed like the whole world had gathered in Bethlehem! There wasn't a single free room at the inn. "No room here," the innkeepers said, spreading their hands. And Mary needed to rest more than ever: her little baby was about to be born.

A kind innkeeper offered them shelter in a stable — the very place where an ox, a little donkey, and some sheep lived. Joseph spread out fresh straw, and it began to feel almost cozy. The animals breathed warm little breaths and looked on so kindly, as if to say, "Guests are always welcome here."

And that very night, the baby was born — Mary's little son. They named him Jesus. His very first bed was a manger, a feeding trough for animals, lined with soft, sweet-smelling hay. Mary sang him the very first lullaby of his life.

Not far away, in a field, some shepherds sat by their fire, watching over their flocks. The night was quiet, so very quiet: the fire crackled softly, and the sheep snored gently. The shepherds had no idea that this night would become the most famous night the world has ever known.

Suddenly the night sky lit up! A warm light spread over the field, and the shepherds heard joyful news: “Don't be afraid! Today a special baby was born in Bethlehem. Go — you will find him in a manger.”

The shepherds dropped everything and ran to the town. And sure enough: there in the stable, in the manger, lay a newborn baby, fast asleep. The shepherds tiptoed closer, and the youngest one brought a little white lamb as a gift. They were the very first visitors.

Far, far away in the east lived three wise stargazers. Every night they studied the sky and knew every little star by name. And then, suddenly — a new star! Bright as a tiny sun. "It's a sign!" the wise men decided. "A great king has been born. Let's go and pay him honor!"

The wise men gathered their gifts, climbed onto their camels, and set off on their journey. By day they rested, and by night they followed the star — it floated across the sky ahead of them, like a guiding little lantern. Many days and nights the journey lasted.

At last the star led them to Bethlehem — and stopped over one humble little house. “Here!” the wise men said, glancing at one another. Not over a palace, not over a fortress — over the plainest little house. Wonders, it seems, choose the simplest places.

The wise men came in, bowed to the baby, and brought out their gifts: shining gold, sweet-smelling frankincense, and precious myrrh. Three gifts—like three wishes: to be generous, to be kind, and to be strong.

The little stable grew warm and crowded: shepherds and wise men, a lamb, and camels just outside the door, an ox and a little donkey. All so different — yet sharing just one joy. That's how it is on the very best of holidays.

The wise men went home by a different road — it was safer that way for the baby. They carried with them not gold, but something far more precious: the memory of the night a star had led them to a miracle.

More than two thousand years have passed since then, and that day is celebrated all around the world — that's Christmas. A tree, a star on top, presents, and family gathered around one table. And it all began with one quiet night, a little manger, and a star.
